title: The armor of God (Ephesians 6:10–17)
hookLine: truth as a belt, faith as a shield, the word as a sword

cards: Someone chained to a Roman soldier for months would come to know his kit by heart. The belt. The breastplate.
The sandals. The tall shield, the helmet, the short sword. Acts says that in Rome Paul lived under guard with a soldier, and in Ephesians he calls himself an ambassador in a chain.
Whether or not he wrote this looking at a guard, the picture he paints at the end of the letter is unmistakable. He dresses the whole church for battle.

teach.b: "Put you on the armour of God, that you may be able to stand against the deceits of the devil." The word for the full armor is panoplia: every piece, head to foot.
Then Paul says who the enemy is: our wrestling is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities and powers and the spirits of wickedness. Not people.
In Paul's picture, the enemy is never the person across the table. Then he hands out the kit, piece by piece. Truth as a belt, holding everything in place.
The breastplate of justice; the Douay-Rheims says justice, following the Latin, where the King James says righteousness. Feet ready with the gospel of peace.
Then "the shield of faith," to quench the fiery darts of the most wicked one. The helmet of salvation. And the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God.

teach.h: ALMOST ALL OF IT IS FOR STANDING.
teach.b: Almost everything in it is for standing, not attacking. Paul's verb is stand, over and over. The only weapon is the sword, and it's made of words: God's word.
Much of this comes from the prophet Isaiah, where God himself puts on justice as a breastplate and a helmet of salvation.

teach.h: PUT ON THE ARMOR OF GOD.
teach.b: So the armor is God's own, lent out. The armor picture lives on in prayer.
An old Irish prayer called Saint Patrick's Breastplate, attributed by tradition to Patrick, asks Christ to surround the one praying on every side, and some people pray it as they start the day.

how: Some Catholics pray a morning offering as they begin the day, and some pray Saint Patrick's Breastplate, a prayer traditionally attributed to Patrick that asks Christ's protection on every side.

games.q: you're handed the armor of God. what does Paul tell you to do in it, again and again?
games.why: stand: against the deceits of the devil, girt with truth, shielded by faith.

practice: Touch your head, helmet; your chest, breastplate; your waist, belt; your feet, shoes; and with each, think one word: hope, justice, truth, peace.

Then name one thing you'll need to stand firm against today, a temptation, a lie, a fear, but not a person. If you pray, pray through Paul's list; if not, let the four touches remind you what you want to carry.

wordCard.voice: Panoplia. Full armor, every piece, head to foot: Paul's picture of the Christian dressed in truth, justice, peace, faith and the word of God. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: put on the armor. Almost all of it is for standing. Day five hundred eighty-six, done.
